what.text: CJC-1295 is a lab-made version of growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH). It is the first 29 amino acids of human GHRH with four amino acids swapped, plus an added lysine with a chemical group that makes it bind to albumin, a protein in the blood. The Canadian company ConjuChem described it in 2005.

src.label: Jetté et al., Endocrinology, 2005

what.text: Binding to albumin makes it last much longer than natural GHRH. In healthy adults its half-life was 5.8 to 8.1 days. Like natural GHRH, it acts on the pituitary gland to release growth hormone, which raises IGF-1.

src.label: Teichman et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab, 2006
Ionescu and Frohman, J Clin Endocrinol Metab, 2006

what.text: What is sold under the name may differ. A product seized in Norway in 2009 and analysed by an anti-doping laboratory contained a 29-amino-acid peptide whose sequence matched the peptide marketed as CJC-1295.

src.label: Henninge et al., Drug Test Anal, 2010

what.text: CJC-1295 is not an approved medicine anywhere we checked. Using it for sleep has not been studied.

research.text: CJC-1295 has been tested in a few small studies in healthy adults, measuring growth hormone and IGF-1. ConjuChem's one Phase II trial was terminated, and no results are posted. We found no study of CJC-1295 and sleep.
Each study is listed below as it was run.

research.title: Dose trials in healthy adults, 2006

facts.v: two randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind, ascending-dose trials. Injections under the skin: single doses in the first trial, 2 or 3 weekly or every-other-week doses in the second.
healthy adults aged 21 to 61 (the abstract does not give the number)
growth hormone, IGF-1, drug levels, safety

research.found: One injection raised average growth hormone 2- to 10-fold for 6 days or more, and IGF-1 1.5- to 3-fold for 9 to 11 days. With repeat doses, IGF-1 stayed above baseline for up to 28 days. No serious adverse reactions were reported.

src.label: Teichman et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab, 2006

research.title: Overnight growth hormone pulses, 2006

facts.v: blood every 20 minutes over one night, before and 1 week after a single injection. No placebo group.

research.found: Growth hormone pulses kept their normal rhythm. Baseline growth hormone rose 7.5-fold, average growth hormone 46% and IGF-1 45%. Sleep was not measured.

src.label: Ionescu and Frohman, J Clin Endocrinol Metab, 2006

research.text: A 2009 analysis of blood from 11 healthy young men, before and a week after one CJC-1295 injection, found changes in several blood proteins. It looked for markers of growth hormone action, not health effects.

src.label: Sackmann-Sala et al., Growth Horm IGF Res, 2009

research.title: HIV-related belly fat, ConjuChem

facts.v: multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled Phase II; low dose, high dose or placebo
planned 120 adults aged 18 to 65 with HIV and excess belly fat
12 weeks of treatment, 6 weeks of follow-up
efficacy, drug levels, safety and tolerability

research.found: The registry lists the trial as terminated, with a completion date of September 2006. It gives no reason and no results.

src.label: NCT00267527, ClinicalTrials.gov

research.text: In rats, CJC-1295 raised growth hormone more than unmodified GHRH(1-29) and stayed in the blood beyond 72 hours. In mice bred without GHRH, daily injections normalized growth. These results are in animals only.

us.text: Not FDA approved for any use. It was in FDA's Category 2 (substances that may pose significant safety risks) before its compounding nominations were withdrawn. It is not on the 503A or 503B bulks lists, and it is not in the HHS peptide policy of October 2026. As of November 1, 2026.

items.text: none. A search of Drugs@FDA found no product with CJC-1295 as an active ingredient, and the only Phase II trial was terminated.

world.lead: CJC-1295 is not approved as a medicine in any country we checked. Canada has seized it, Australia makes it prescription-only and illegal to hold without authority, and WADA bans it at all times.

after.title: Sport
after.text: CJC-1295 is prohibited at all times (in and out of competition) under WADA class S2.2.4, growth hormone releasing factors. The class names "growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) and its analogues (e.g. CJC-1293, CJC-1295, sermorelin and tesamorelin)." All substances in class S2 are non-Specified. It is still named in the same class on the 2027 list, which takes effect January 1, 2027.

unconfirmed: The reason ConjuChem's Phase II trial (NCT00267527) was terminated is not given in the registry, and no results are posted.
FDA's Category 2 page does not give the date CJC-1295 was added or say which nomination (503A or 503B) it was under.
The number of people in the 2006 healthy-adult dose trials is not given in the abstract.
We could not open an FDA record describing the adverse event reports behind FDA's Category 2 statement.
Status in the UK was not checked against a regulator record.
surprises: FDA names serious adverse events for CJC-1295, increased heart rate and a systemic vasodilatory reaction, although the published trials in healthy adults reported none.
The CJC-1295 described in trials has an extra albumin-binding lysine group; a product sold under that name and seized in Norway contained a 29-amino-acid peptide.
We found no published study of CJC-1295 and sleep, and no trial of it for any sleep problem.
